title: Effects and loading data
intro: React components are mainly about describing UI, but applications also need to interact with the world outside React. In this lesson, you will learn how useEffect handles side effects such as timers and data fetching, how cleanup works, and how to model loading, success, and error states.
takeaways: useEffect is used to synchronise a React component with external systems such as APIs, timers, subscriptions, and browser APIs.
The dependency array controls when an effect runs: no array means every render, an empty array means initial setup, and values mean the effect reacts to those values changing.
Effects that create timers, subscriptions, or cancellable requests should return a cleanup function that stops or disconnects them.
Data fetching should model loading, success, and error states and should account for repeated requests and race conditions.
For larger applications, libraries such as TanStack Query can handle many data-fetching concerns, but understanding effects first makes those abstractions much easier to use.

quiz.question: What is a side effect in a React component?
options: Calculating a value from two numbers
Returning JSX from a component
Interacting with something outside React, such as a timer or network request
Using a CSS class
quiz.explanation: Side effects are operations that interact with systems outside React's rendering calculation, such as fetching data, starting timers, or subscribing to events.

quiz.question: When does this effect normally run in production?
options: useEffect(() => { console.log("Hello"); }, []);
After every render
Only when a prop called value changes
After the component mounts, because it has an empty dependency array
quiz.explanation: An empty dependency array means the effect does not depend on changing values, so it runs after the component mounts in normal production behaviour.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of returning a function from useEffect?
options: To render a second component
To provide cleanup for the effect
To change the dependency array
To prevent the component from rendering
quiz.explanation: The returned function is the effect's cleanup function. It can clear timers, unsubscribe from events, or abort requests when the effect is no longer active.

quiz.question: Why can fetching data in an effect without a dependency array be dangerous?
options: The browser cannot make network requests from React
The effect can run after every render and repeatedly trigger requests
The response can never contain JSON
React automatically disables fetch
quiz.explanation: Without a dependency array, an effect runs after every render. If it fetches data and updates state, that update can trigger another render and another request.

quiz.question: What problem can AbortController help with when an effect fetches data based on a changing search term?
options: It converts JSON into JSX
It prevents all network errors
It can cancel an outdated request when the effect is cleaned up
It automatically caches every response
quiz.explanation: AbortController can cancel a request when its effect is cleaned up, helping prevent older requests from continuing after a newer search has started.

exercise.title: Load and reload tasks
exercise.task: Build an `App` component that loads tasks from the provided `window.api.getTasks()` function when the component mounts. Keep the exact `window.api` starter definition at the top of the code. While a request is running, render a paragraph with `data-testid="loading"` containing exactly `Loading…`; after a successful request, render a `ul` with `data-testid="task-list"` containing one `li` for each task title. If the request rejects, render an element with `role="alert"` containing `Could not load tasks`. Add a `Reload` button that starts the request again and shows the loading state while it is running. The tests wait with `await tick(150)`, and one test replaces `window.api.getTasks` with a rejecting function before clicking `Reload`, so the component must call the API function each time it loads.
exercise.hint: Keep separate state for the tasks, loading status, and error status. Put the request in a reusable loadTasks function, call it from an effect on mount, and use the same function for the Reload button. The UI can use loading first, then choose between the error message and task list.
